Piwniczna-Zdroj Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Piwniczna-Zdrój, Poland

Not demolished. Piwniczna, a royal city founded in 1348, had no Jewish residents recorded until settlement began in the 18th century, facing early opposition from Christian burghers and possibly a royal ban. Larger settlement came in the second half of the 19th century, though Jews never exceeded 8% of the population; the local community remained affiliated with Nowy Sącz's Jewish community despite establishing its own institutions. About 230 Jews lived there before WWII; Germans expelled them in fall 1940 to the Stary Sącz and Nowy Sącz ghettos, both liquidated in spring 1942 with deportations to Bełżec and Treblinka. This cemetery, likely founded toward the end of the 19th century near the Poprad River, had its stones used by German occupiers to harden pavement outside a gendarmerie station; a dozen recovered matzevot were returned and the site fenced in the 1970s.
